data.title: Minimum Window Substring
data.summary:
Input: Two strings s and t.
Output: The minimum length substring of s that contains every character in t with the required frequencies, or an empty string if no such window exists.
Rules: If there are multiple such windows, any valid minimum window will be accepted.
constraints: s and t consist of uppercase and lowercase English letters.

data.generator_code:
import random

def generate(rng, n):
    alphabet = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"
    s = ''.join(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(n))
    t_len = rng.randint(1, min(n, 20))
    t = ''.join(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(t_len))
    return [s, t]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    s = 'a' * n
    t = 'a' * min(n, 10)
    return [s, t]

data.key_insight: We can expand a right pointer to build a window until all required characters from t are present with sufficient frequency, then contract a left pointer to find the minimal valid window size before expanding again.

steps.title: Count Target Frequencies
steps.detail: Build a frequency map of characters in string t and count the number of unique characters that need to be satisfied.

steps.title: Expand Window with Right Pointer
steps.detail: Iterate through s with a right pointer, adding characters to the current window frequency map. Track how many unique target characters have reached their required target frequency.

steps.title: Contract Window with Left Pointer
steps.detail: Whenever all required character frequencies are satisfied, record the current window length if it is smaller than the minimum found so far. Then advance the left pointer to shrink the window until it is no longer valid.

steps.title: Extract Minimum Window Substring
steps.detail: Return the smallest substring recorded during the sliding process, or an empty string if no valid window was found.

data.pattern_summary: The Sliding Window pattern uses two pointers to maintain a dynamic range or window over an array or string, adjusting the window boundaries to find a subsegment that meets specific conditions efficiently.

pattern_options.name: Sliding Window
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We need to find a contiguous substring in s that meets a condition, and we can adjust the window bounds dynamically.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. This problem asks for a contiguous substring based on character counts rather than optimal substructure or overlapping subproblems of a sequence.

pattern_options.name: Binary Search
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. While we could potentially binary search for the window length, checking validity takes linear time and does not easily yield the exact window.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. A purely greedy local choice does not guarantee finding the minimum window length without tracking both ends.

signals.hint: Mentioning a substring of variable length strongly points toward a window approach.

signals.phrase: contains every character in t with the required frequencies
signals.hint: Checking content validity inside a changing range suggests expanding and contracting boundaries.

data.brute_force_idea: The brute-force approach generates every possible substring of s, checks if each substring contains all characters of t with the required frequencies, and keeps track of the shortest valid substring found.
data.brute_force_why: There are O(n^2) substrings, and for each substring, building its frequency counter and checking against t takes O(n) or O(m) time.
data.bottleneck: Slicing the string and re-counting character frequencies from scratch for every single pair of start and end indices creates massive redundant work.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times substrings are created and measured from scratch.
Notice that when you move the start or end index by one position, most of the characters in the substring remain the same.
Ask yourself if you really need to rebuild the character count for a new window using a completely fresh loop.

data.overview: The algorithm uses a sliding window approach with two pointers, left and right. It expands the right pointer to include characters until all requirements of t are met, and then contracts the left pointer to find the minimum valid window.
data.intuition: Imagine holding a flexible measuring tape over a string. You stretch the right end forward until you have caught all the required item types, then you pull the left end up as far as possible without losing any items.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach repeatedly scans overlapping substrings to check character frequencies, leading to redundant work. The sliding window pattern removes this bottleneck by maintaining a single dynamic window using two pointers (left and right), expanding right to include new characters and contracting left once all required characters from t are found.

derivation.note: Constructs the frequency map for t once at the beginning.
The right pointer iterates through each character of s exactly once.
The left pointer only moves forward and never backtracks across the entire execution.

data.time_summary: Building the target frequency map takes O(|t|) time. The right pointer traverses s of length |s| once, and the left pointer also traverses s at most once. Because each pointer moves forward at most |s| times, the total time complexity is O(|s| + |t|), which is confirmed by the near-linear step growth.
data.space_summary: The space complexity is O(|s| + |t|) because the hash maps store at most the distinct characters present in strings s and t, bounded by the character set size.
data.takeaway: When a problem asks for a minimum or maximum subarray/substring satisfying a condition, use a sliding window with two pointers to expand and contract dynamically rather than re-evaluating every possible substring.
mistakes: Forgetting to check whether a dictionary key exists before updating or comparing counts.
Failing to advance the left pointer correctly once the window condition is met, leading to missed smaller valid windows.
Confusing total character counts with the count of distinct unique characters required.
